B08_00: Alkylation damage such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine blocks base pairing and stalls replication. ALKBH2, an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase related to bacterial AlkB, hydroxylates the methyl group so it leaves as formaldehyde, restoring the base directly without excision or strand breakage; ethyl adducts leave as acetaldehyde. Working mainly on double-stranded DNA at replication foci, it protects genome integrity and influences sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy.
B08_01: Abasic sites, formed spontaneously or by glycosylases removing damaged bases, must be processed before they cause mutations or breaks. In this AP-endonuclease-independent branch of base excision repair, the bifunctional glycosylases NEIL1 and NEIL2 incise the strand, leaving 3' phosphate and 5' deoxyribose phosphate ends. PNKP removes the 3' phosphate, DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP and inserts one nucleotide, and XRCC1-LIG3 seals the nick, limiting mutagenesis from oxidative lesions.
B08_02: Base excision repair commits when DNA glycosylases hydrolyse the N-glycosidic bond of an oxidised or alkylated purine, leaving an abasic site for downstream repair. OGG1 removes 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes adenine mispaired opposite it, MPG handles alkylated and deaminated purines, and NEIL3 acts on further oxidised lesions, operating in chromatin and at telomeres. Unrepaired 8-oxoguanine causes G:C to T:A transversions, and MUTYH loss causes inherited polyposis and colorectal cancer.
B08_03: When replication stalls at a UV-induced thymine dimer, DNA polymerase eta copies across it accurately, inserting two adenines; RPA coats the single strand, RFC loads PCNA, and monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the polymerase. SPRTN and the VCP/p97 segregase with UFD1-NPLOC4, using ubiquitin, then remove the enzyme to restore replicative synthesis. Loss of polymerase eta causes variant xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme photosensitivity and early skin cancer from error-prone bypass.
B08_04: Damaged pyrimidines from oxidation and deamination are excised in the first committed step of base excision repair, when glycosylases cleave the N-glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site. The enzymes include uracil glycosylases UNG and SMUG1, mismatch glycosylases TDG and MBD4, and oxidised-pyrimidine enzymes NTHL1 and the NEIL family. Acting on nucleosomal DNA and at telomeres alongside shelterin proteins, this step prevents C-to-T mutations, cancer predisposition and chromosome-end damage.
B08_05: In global genome nucleotide excision repair, dual incision releases bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts after DDB1-DDB2 and PARP1/PARP2 mark the damage and XPA, RPA and TFIIH open a bubble. ERCC1-ERCC4 cuts 5' and ERCC5 cuts 3' of the lesion, excising a 27-30 nucleotide fragment, and RFC, PCNA and polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa fill the gap. Defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum with sun sensitivity and skin cancer.
B08_06: During homologous recombination, the presynaptic step builds the RAD51 nucleoprotein filament that searches for a sister template. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP and other nucleases resect breaks into RPA-coated 3' tails; BRCA2 with BRCA1-BARD1, under ATM, ATR and CHEK1 signalling, replaces RPA with RAD51, and RAD51 paralogues stabilise the filament while the 9-1-1 clamp sustains checkpoint signalling. Loss causes chromosomal instability, hereditary breast, ovarian and Fanconi-type cancer predisposition, and PARP-inhibitor sensitivity.
B08_07: DNA glycosylases that excise damaged or mismatched bases bind their abasic product tightly, so the AP endonuclease APEX1 must displace them and take over the lesion before cutting the backbone. This handoff shields the mutagenic, replication-blocking abasic site and channels intermediates between enzymes. The glycosylases cover oxidised guanine and thymine, alkylated purines, uracil and mismatches, and inherited defects such as MUTYH deficiency predispose to colorectal adenomas and cancer.
B08_08: Synthesis-dependent strand annealing lets homologous recombination repair a double-strand break without crossover: after extension on the sister template, the invading strand is displaced from the D-loop by RTEL1 and reanneals with its partner, avoiding loss of heterozygosity. Upstream, MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and the BLM dissolvasome resect ends, and BRCA1-BARD1, PALB2 and BRCA2 load RAD51; gaps are filled and ligated. Defects cause breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.
B08_09: Microhomology-mediated end joining is a mutagenic backup for double-strand break repair, relied on by homologous recombination-deficient tumours such as BRCA-mutant cancers, making polymerase theta and PARP drug targets. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP performs limited resection; PARP1/2 and POLQ align ends at short microhomologies, POLQ extends them, FEN1 trims flaps and LIG3-XRCC1 seals nicks. Products always carry deletions, often base substitutions and occasionally translocations.
B08_10: The final stage of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair fills and seals the gap left after a lesion stalling RNA polymerase II is excised, so transcription can resume. RPA coats the gap, RFC loads PCNA, polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa synthesise the patch, and ligase I or ligase III-XRCC1 seals it, with CSA, CSB, UVSSA and TFIIH present. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with degeneration of non-dividing cells.
B08_11: Long-patch base excision repair is used when a nick's 5' end resists one-nucleotide patching, mainly in S phase. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, polymerase beta adds a nucleotide, RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta or epsilon performs strand-displacement synthesis with RPA on the flap; FEN1 removes the flap and DNA ligase I seals it. This links repair of oxidative and alkylation damage to the replication machinery.
B08_12: Translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase kappa lets stalled forks continue past oxidised bases such as thymine glycol and 8-oxoguanine and past polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon adducts, preventing fork breakage at the cost of mutations. Recruitment needs RFC-loaded PCNA monoubiquitinated with ubiquitin from UBB, UBC and ribosomal fusion genes, plus RPA. POLK cooperates with REV1 and polymerase zeta (REV3L-MAD2L2), which extends past the lesion, making this damage tolerance rather than repair.
B08_13: Double-strand break responses are damped by degrading the BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer, which drives homologous recombination and resection. Cullin4-RBX1-DDB1 ligases with DCAF8L1 or DCAF8L2 as substrate receptors polyubiquitinate BRCA1-BARD1, which the 26S proteasome then degrades. This turnover restrains recombination, influences repair pathway choice and limits checkpoint duration; because BRCA1-BARD1 loss causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, it also affects genome stability and tumour sensitivity to break-inducing agents.
B08_14: Damage recognition in global genome nucleotide excision repair scans the whole genome for bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts. XPC with RAD23A/B and centrin-2 detects destabilised pairing, while the UV-DDB ligase (DDB2, DDB1, cullin-4, RBX1) binds the lesion and retains XPC; COP9-modulated ubiquitination, PARP1/2 and INO80 remodelling make the site accessible. This step precedes incision and resynthesis, and its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum with sun sensitivity and skin cancer.
B08_15: ALKBH3 directly reverses 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, alkylation lesions that block pairing and stall replication, restoring the base in one oxidative step without excision. This iron(II)- and alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase hydroxylates the methyl group, releasing formaldehyde, or acetaldehyde from ethyl adducts. Preferring single-stranded DNA, it relies on the ASCC complex, whose ASCC3 helicase unwinds duplexes and ASCC1/ASCC2 target damage, contributing to alkylation tolerance and tumour responses to methylating chemotherapy.
B08_16: O6-methylguanine, produced by endogenous or chemotherapeutic alkylating agents, pairs with cytosine or thymine and causes G:C to A:T transitions. MGMT reverses it directly by transferring the methyl group to its own active-site cysteine, which inactivates the protein so repair capacity depends on protein amount. MGMT promoter hypermethylation in glioma and other tumours raises mutational load but sensitises tumours to temozolomide, making MGMT status a prognostic and predictive oncology marker.
B08_17: Short-patch base excision repair clears the abasic site left after a glycosylase excises a damaged base, preventing persistent mutagenic, replication-blocking lesions from oxidative and alkylation damage. APEX1 displaces the glycosylase and incises 5' of the abasic sugar, producing a nick with a 3'-hydroxyl. DNA polymerase beta is recruited and its lyase activity removes the 5'-deoxyribose phosphate, leaving a clean one-nucleotide gap ready for fill-in synthesis and ligation.
B08_18: A double-strand break is converted into a checkpoint and repair signal when MRN senses ends and activates ATM, which phosphorylates H2AX; gamma-H2AX spreads and docks MDC1 to form foci. RNF8, RNF168 and HERC2 ubiquitinate histones to recruit RAP80 and BRCA1-A, while KDM4A/B removal and NSD2-mediated H4K20 methylation allow 53BP1 binding. ATM phosphorylates BRCA1-BARD1, 53BP1 and CHEK2, driving TP53 arrest; defects cause radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and breast and ovarian cancer.
B08_19: D-loops and double Holliday junctions formed in homologous recombination must be removed before segregation, and the route decides the genetic outcome. BLM-TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 dissolves junctions into non-crossovers, whereas GEN1, SLX1A-SLX4 and MUS81-EME1/EME2 cleave them into crossovers that risk loss of heterozygosity. Upstream resection, ATM signalling and RAD51 loading by BRCA1-BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 provide context, with SPIDR and FIGNL1-FIRRM favouring non-crossovers; mutations underlie Bloom syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
B08_20: This first step of double-strand break detection begins when MRE11-RAD50-NBN binds and tethers broken ends, triggering KAT5 to acetylate ATM, which autophosphorylates and converts from inactive dimer to active monomer. Active ATM then phosphorylates targets that arrest the cell cycle and recruit repair factors, coupling detection to the damage response, with karyopherins importing components into the nucleus. Defects cause ataxia-telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage and MRE11-deficiency syndromes with immunodeficiency and cancer predisposition.
B08_21: Dual incision in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair cuts out a bulky lesion that has stalled RNA polymerase II. The polymerase first backtracks, aided by ERCC6, ERCC8-dependent ubiquitination, UVSSA, TCEA1-stimulated RNA cleavage and TFIIH helicases; then ERCC1-ERCC4 incises 5' and ERCC5 3' of the lesion on a substrate stabilised by XPA and RPA, leaving a gap refilled by PCNA-dependent polymerases. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with photosensitivity and neurodegeneration.
B08_22: After error-prone Y-family polymerases bypass a lesion, translesion synthesis must be terminated to restore accurate replication and limit mutations carried into daughter cells. Deubiquitinases such as USP10 remove ubiquitin from PCNA, evicting polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1 so that polymerases delta and epsilon, loaded by RFC on RPA-coated template, resume. An ISG15 arm via UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25 modifies PCNA and PCLAF, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to fork restart.
B08_23: Base excision repair starts when a glycosylase flips out an aberrant base; this step covers recognition of damaged or mismatched pyrimidines arising from oxidation, deamination and alkylation. UNG and SMUG1 handle uracil, TDG and MBD4 handle mismatched thymine at CpG sites, NTHL1 and NEIL enzymes oxidised pyrimidines, and OGG1 oxidised purines. Recognition occurs in chromatin and at telomeres, and germline glycosylase defects cause point mutations and cancer predisposition.
B08_24: Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks by direct religation without a template, functions throughout the cycle especially in G1, and seals V(D)J recombination breaks; defects cause radiosensitivity and severe combined immunodeficiency. MRN activates ATM, H2AX phosphorylation and RNF8/RNF168/UBE2N signalling recruit 53BP1 with RIF1 and PAXIP1 to block resection. Ku70/Ku80 with DNA-PKcs synapses ends, ARTEMIS, TDP1 and TDP2 process them, polymerases mu and lambda fill gaps, and XRCC4-LIG4-XLF ligates.
B08_25: Global genome nucleotide excision repair assembles an incision complex to excise bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts. After XPC and UV-DDB mark the damage, TFIIH is recruited, its ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases open a bubble, XPA verifies the lesion and RPA protects the undamaged strand; ERCC5 and ERCC1-ERCC4 then dock to cut. PARP1/2, CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 and SUMO modification tune assembly, and defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum with skin cancer.
B08_26: When a single-nucleotide patch cannot complete base excision repair, a long-patch route displaces and removes a short flap, preventing persistent single-strand breaks. After APEX1 incision, polymerase beta synthesises about two to ten nucleotides by strand displacement, FEN1 cleaves the flap and DNA ligase I seals it. PARP1 and PARP2 sense breaks and make poly(ADP-ribose) to recruit factors, PARG and ADPRS reverse it, and PARP inhibitors exploit this step.
B08_27: End resection commits a double-strand break to homology-directed repair by producing long 3' single-stranded tails. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1 initiate trimming, and EXO1 or DNA2 with BLM or WRN extend it; CDK2-cyclin A limits this to S and G2, while ATM and RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin and SUMO marks organise recruitment. RPA-coated tails activate ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1, RAD17-RFC and 9-1-1 to signal through CHEK1; defects cause instability and breast and ovarian cancer.
B08_28: In transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, a pre-incision complex forms at RNA polymerase II stalled on a lesion to verify damage and open DNA. ERCC6 (CSB) recruits ERCC8 (CSA) in a CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome, UVSSA brings USP7 to stabilise ERCC6, and XPA with TFIIH helicases unwinds DNA while XAB2 and TCEA1 aid polymerase backtracking. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with neurodegeneration rather than cancer.
B08_29: Interstrand crosslinks block replication and transcription. In this route the glycosylase NEIL3 unhooks certain crosslinks, such as psoralen- and abasic-site-derived ones, by cleaving one glycosidic bond, turning the crosslink into single-strand lesions manageable by base excision repair and replication. Acting at stalled forks without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, it avoids double-strand break intermediates and offers a rapid, low-risk first option, with Fanconi anaemia repair as backup.
B08_30: REV1-mediated translesion synthesis allows replication past lesions such as abasic sites that would otherwise stall and collapse forks. REV1 inserts a C opposite the damage as a dCMP transferase and serves as a scaffold; monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by RFC onto RPA-coated DNA, promotes its recruitment. Polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2, which binds REV1) then extends past the lesion with low fidelity, preserving survival at the cost of point mutations.
B08_31: DNA polymerase iota lets stalled forks continue past lesions that replicative polymerases cannot copy, preventing fork collapse and cell death while adding mutations. POLI favours Hoogsteen pairing, flipping template purines into the syn conformation to read adducted or edge-damaged G and A. It is recruited by monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by RFC onto RPA-coated DNA, with REV1 as scaffold, and because it extends poorly, polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2) completes extension.
B08_32: Single strand annealing is a mutagenic double-strand break repair route that pairs repeated sequences, deleting one repeat and the intervening DNA, reshaping tumour genomes when recombination fails. ATM activation and extensive resection by MRN with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1, then EXO1 or DNA2 with BLM and WRN, create RPA-coated tails that trigger ATR checkpoint signalling. ABL1-phosphorylated RAD52 anneals the repeats and blocks RAD51, ERCC1-ERCC4 trims flaps, and ligation completes repair.
B08_33: When replicative polymerases stall at DNA lesions, the fork signals this and switches to translesion polymerases, preventing collapse into double-strand breaks but introducing mutations seen in tumours. With PCNA and polymerase delta or epsilon held by the clamp loader and single-strand binding protein, RAD18-UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA, weakening replicative polymerase binding and recruiting Y-family polymerases. A DDB1-DTL cullin-RING ligase also modifies PCNA, and USP1-WDR48 deubiquitination limits error-prone synthesis.
B08_34: Base excision repair of oxidised and alkylated purines begins when a specific glycosylase scans the minor groove, kinks the DNA and flips the damaged base into its active site, cleaving the N-glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site. OGG1 removes 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes adenine opposite it, MPG alkylpurines and NEIL3 hydantoins, within chromatin and at telomeres. Loss raises mutation rates, and MUTYH deficiency predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis.
B08_35: The last stage of global genome nucleotide excision repair restores intact DNA after a bulky lesion is excised. The 27-30 nucleotide gap is held by RPA, RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta, epsilon or kappa refills it; LIG1 seals nicks in replicating cells, whereas LIG3-XRCC1 does so in non-cycling cells, with ubiquitin supporting PCNA modification. Without it single-strand breaks persist, and repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum and sunlight-induced cancer.
